The Information：Anthropic 在准备一款新模型，话说一半它也能猜到你要什么

科技媒体 The Information 10 月 19 日在 AI Agenda 通讯里报道，Anthropic 正在准备一款新模型，推理能力和“直觉”比目前对外提供的模型都强。消息来自一位用过这款模型的人，Anthropic 没有公开回应。

这位知情人提到两个变化。

第一，它更会揣摩用户没说出口的意图。你只给很少的信息，它也能看出你真正想达到什么目的。报道里的例子是写代码：你让它修一个 bug，它可能会顺藤摸瓜，找出导致这个 bug 的一整类问题，再问你要不要一起修掉。

第二，它更少给套路化的答案。原文例子是：用户问怎么炒股，它不会只说“看看市盈率”这种人人都知道的建议，可能会自己设计一套算法去预测股价走势。这套算法预测得准不准，报道没说，这只是用来说明它的回答方式。

对普通用户来说，这意味着提示词可以写得更随意，不用把需求一条条交代清楚。对写代码的人来说，模型可能会主动扩大修改范围，好处是一次修到根上，代价是你得多花点心思审查它改了什么。

什么时候能用、叫什么名字？目前都没有确定说法。据原推 TestingCatalog 说，新模型这个月就会发布，但还不清楚会归入 Fable 还是 Opus 系列。Google 在做 Gemini 4 Carbon，是上周刚推出的 Gemini 4 Argon 的升级版；OpenAI 在准备 Terra 系列的新模型，可能几周内发布，能力有提升，价格会比 GPT-6.1 Sol 低。

原文：https://www.theinformation.com/newsletters/ai-agenda/anthropic-readies-model-reads-users-intentions-better

quoted_tweet.author: 🚨 AI News | TestingCatalog
quoted_tweet.text:
ANTHROPIC 🔥: According to The Information, Anthropic will release a new model this month, along with Gemini 4 Carbon and a new Terra model from OpenAI. 

> "The unreleased model is especially good at discerning a person’s underlying intentions and goals even if they don’t give the model much information."

> "The Anthropic model is also better at thinking outside of the box rather than regurgitating common sense advice or solutions."

> "It’s not clear which model family Anthropic will fall into, such as Fable or Opus."

Thinking outside of the box is a huge limitation these days. If we get a model that can do it reliably, we'll be properly transitioning into the "Innovators" stage. 

The line about "discerning underlying intentions" is a bit scary, though, given all the guardrails.

ChatGPT Slides 能多人一起改幻灯片了，Pro、Business 和企业版可用

OpenAI 给 ChatGPT 的幻灯片功能 ChatGPT Slides 加了两项新能力：多人实时协作，以及直接在幻灯片上点着改。

简单测试了一下，体验挺好的，在线编辑很方便。

协作的用法和在线文档差不多。做好的幻灯片可以分享给同事，几个人同时在 ChatGPT 里编辑，在页面上留评论。评论攒多了，可以让 ChatGPT 或者你的 dot 按评论把幻灯片改一遍。dot 是 OpenAI 上个月在开发者大会上发布的 AI agent，有自己的云端电脑和浏览器，能在后台长时间替你干活。

编辑方面，现在可以直接点到幻灯片上改文字、更新图表，拖动或缩放图片和形状。改个错别字、挪张图这种小事，自己动手就行，不必每次都打字让 ChatGPT 去改。

用法是在对话里，或者针对你上传的文件，对 ChatGPT 说“create ChatGPT slides”（生成 ChatGPT 幻灯片）。做好后可以直接在 ChatGPT 里放映，也能导出成 PowerPoint 或 Google Slides 文件接着改。

这些功能目前只对 Pro、Business 和 Enterprise 用户开放，公告没有提到免费版和 Plus。

官方介绍：http://chatgpt.com/features/slides/

What has to go right for AI to actually show up as positive in your P&L:

- Having the right sponsors: someone from the C suite, with a budget that they can spend and, very importantly, the involvement of the owners of the processes that you're going to be automating. And, also, the early involvement of key stakeholders, like legal, information security, IT, and finance.

- Really understanding the as-is processes that you're going to be automating: this requires process mining of the systems of record, and an understanding of the detail of each process, who's involved, all of the variations, and the volumes and the cycle times.

- Understanding the baseline of the process and the metric that you're going to measure to understand how much value you're creating: are you looking at time saved, cost saved, revenue increased after spending the tokens, or risk reduced, and agreeing the key KPIs that you're going to measure.

- Re-engineering the processes, as you automate them. Usually, you'll end up with about five steps, of which four of them will be automated using AI. And use plain code wherever plain code works.

- Building AI agents that work with all of the systems that you've already got in place, like Salesforce, NetSuite, SAP, ServiceNow, Dynamics, et cetera, so that you don't have to move to a new system, or have people log into a new system. And having one architecture layer underneath all of those AI agents.

- Deciding which decisions that the AI agent can make versus where you need human input, and making that decision based on both the risk and the cycle time to make the decision. The agent proposes, a person makes the call, and every action is reversible and traceable.

- Running the AI agents in shadow mode, in live with your volumes, and comparing their output to the people doing the process now. And not paying out anything they produce until you're absolutely sure that the AI agents are doing what they're supposed to be doing.

- Identifying the 5% to 10% of your people who are already using AI, and getting them to be the AI ambassadors and evangelists, and then training all of your people on how they work with the AI agents, and explaining how their jobs will change.

- Having a plan for 7 months from now, where you own all of the AI agents that have been developed, all of the data, all of the evaluations, all of the logs, they're all in your cloud, and they're built to be agnostic to any particular AI model.

Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, on the question that made him kill his first startup despite nearly $1M in first-year revenue: can you outrun the incumbents using the same technology?

"After one year, we had what I would describe as a good business pre-AI... But post-AI, this was not gonna be a venture scale company."

"We realized that the incumbents were gonna be able to use the technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than we could grab market share. That's like a key thing if you're a founder you have to think about."

"Your advantage if you're a new entrant is you're faster moving, you can build a different product, you can use different go-to-market approaches, but there's a ticking clock on the wall."

"It felt for tax like we wouldn't be able to get to hundreds of millions of revenue before our competitors, the incumbents could, because you can only sell tax once a year... It's rare for people to brag about their tax prep situation."

@jgreze @arampell

quoted_tweet.author: a16z
quoted_tweet.text:
Jean-Denis Greze was CTO of Plaid. His next startup, an AI tax product for small businesses, brought in nearly $1M in revenue its first year, and he projected $2.5 to $3M the next. He shut it down anyway.

The reason: in the age of AI, it was never going to be venture scale. Incumbents could use the same technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than a startup could win market share. Tax is also sold once a year, so he had about a one-month window to pivot before the door closed.

The pivot became Town, an AI assistant that works from your email and calendar. It found product-market fit fast enough that Ben Horowitz messaged a16z's Alex Rampell to say it "changed my life."

In this conversation, Alex and Jean-Denis cover:

- How to know when to kill a business that's working on paper
- Why Town competes with OpenAI and Anthropic, the companies it buys its tokens from
- Why the "forward deployed engineer" model gets worse as AI gets better
- How a $1/month AI routine can save a restaurant thousands
- What agents mean for Amazon, advertising and the future of shopping

quoted_tweet.text:
Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, on the question every AI app founder gets asked: what stops the big labs from crushing you?

"It is risky always to be competing with your suppliers, right? We're competing against our suppliers. So you gotta ask yourself, is that naturally the right state of the world?"

"Someone at OpenAI, at Anthropic, at Google could wake up and decide to do that. So the better answer actually is to think about our customers and what they want."

"It is our job to determine from all the AI capabilities, frontier model, open weight, what is the right thing for you as a business. And I think you can save money there, but also you can de-risk ever having made the wrong partner."

"There are companies that picked OpenAI like two years ago, and then Anthropic was better at coding for a 12-month period. And those companies had to use both because they realized to be competitive, they needed Claude."

"If you're a smart business, you really think about the neutrality of who's providing intelligence for you and who's routing."

@jgreze @arampell

text:
Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, argues AI isn't diffusing because most people aren't tinkerers: a text box isn't enough, so the product must both identify the value prop and perform the work for them.

"There's this business that rents surfboards on an island to people and then uses Town to inspect surfboards and little beach buggies, whether they've been damaged, to decide whether afterwards the person should get their deposit back."

"What makes it work there is the tinkerer... The unlock is, is there someone over there that gets AI enough to wanna tinker a solution to their problem?"

"And the problem with that is that there aren't enough tinkerers in the world, or there aren't enough people that have the time to be tinkerers to help their business. And I think that's why AI is not diffusing."

"Instead what you're doing is you're using [AI tools] as a replacement, as like a better Google search."

"If you can make a non-tinkerer into getting the same value as a tinkerer... you could be a ginormous business today because AI can solve so many business problems. You don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there."

@jgreze @arampell

text:
Steven Sinofsky on why it's so hard to diffuse AI into companies: most work runs on know-how that's hard to turn into step-by-step instructions for an agent.

"Algorithmic thinking is really, really, really hard for the vast majority of people who have jobs."

"If you were to go to any person and ask them to create a flow chart for a particular thing that they have to go do, they would probably fail at producing that flow chart."

"Say doing a marketing plan and there's 50 marketing people working on a giant product line. One person probably understands and could document the flow chart."

"So if you put one of these agents in front of people to create these things, their ability to explain to it what to do is really, really limited."

"You're basically just developing the next abstraction layer for how people interact. And developing an abstraction layer has historically, at each level of the abstraction layer, been a highly skilled, very specific individual within an organization."

@stevesi
